name: AD8203YRMZ
title: Single-supply difference amplifier with −6 V to +30 V input common-mode range
summary: A difference amplifier on one supply rail, for current sensing in automotive circuits: it amplifies a small differential voltage while its inputs sit anywhere from −6 V to +30 V on a 5 V supply. Gain is 14, split as a ×7 preamplifier and a ×2 buffer joined through an accessible 100 kΩ resistor, so one or two capacitors make a 1-pole or 2-pole low-pass filter and external resistors change the gain. It runs from 3.5 V to 12 V over −40°C to +125°C, in MSOP-8 or SOIC-8.

circuits.title: High Line Current Sensor
circuits.description: A 14 V battery feeds an inductive load whose return runs through a four-terminal shunt and then a low-side power switch to common. A clamp diode runs from the switch node back to the battery; its conduction sets the common-mode voltage when the switch is off. The two sense terminals of the shunt go to +IN and -IN, so the inputs ride at anywhere from near common (switch on) to above the battery (switch off). A1 and A2 are tied and a capacitor to common forms a single-pole filter with the internal 100 kΩ resistor.

circuits.title: Low Line Current Sensor
circuits.description: The power switch sits on the battery side, with the shunt and inductive load below it and the load returning to common; the clamp diode runs from common up to the switch node. In this arrangement the inputs withstand voltages below ground. Sense terminals go to +IN and -IN; A1 and A2 are tied with a filter capacitor to common.

circuits.title: 4 to 20 mA Current Loop Receiver
circuits.description: The loop current passes through a 10 Ω shunt (R2) between the loop supply and the current source. -IN takes the low end of the shunt directly; +IN takes the high end through a second 10 Ω resistor (R1), so both inputs see the same source resistance and a large shunt does not spoil the common-mode rejection. A1 and A2 are tied with a filter capacitor to ground.

circuits.title: Recommended Circuit for Driving CMOS A/D
circuits.description: A 1 kΩ / 0.01 µF lag network between OUT and a microcontroller's sampling A/D input; the converter reads the capacitor node. The capacitor absorbs the charge kicked back at each sample, which would otherwise deflect the output for some time through the 21 kΩ open-loop output impedance; the network has a time constant of about 10 µs.

operation.text: Two stages: a ×7 preamplifier (A1) built as a dynamic bridge, and a ×2 buffer (A2) with matched 10 kΩ feedback resistors. A1 reaches pin 3 through a 100 kΩ series resistor, so a filter or gain network can sit between the stages, and a half-scale filtered signal is brought back to full scale by A2. Input networks and buffer feedback resistors are ratio-trimmed.

Matched resistor attenuators on pins 1 and 8 keep A1's inputs inside the supply even when the inputs go above +VS or below ground. Equal signals on both inputs leave the bridge balanced and A1's output at zero. A third amplifier, A3, senses the common-mode level at A1 and drives the matched RCM resistors to shrink and offset the range A1 sees, which lets the inputs go below ground and reduces how much the differential signal is attenuated. Because the signal is attenuated then amplified, A1 runs at a higher noise gain, scaling its offset and noise as referred to the inputs.
Input resistance is nominally 320 kΩ. The output stage is open-collector and sources current, swinging to within 20 mV of ground and 200 mV of VS.

A2 bias current is 40 nA typical, seen through about 100 kΩ of source resistance, so mismatch errors are small. It rises when A2 is driven into saturation, for example with VCC/2 at its input; the full-scale output for correct operation is 200 mV below VCC.

A resistor from the tied A1/A2 node to ground lowers the gain without changing bandwidth, with a small offset from the unequal source resistance at the buffer input that a series resistor in pin 4 can null. A resistor from OUT to that node raises the gain; at high gains its accuracy depends closely on the resistor, and the input-referred offset, about six times A1's own, limits dc-coupled high-gain use.
At gains other than 14, one stage clips first, near VS − 0.2 V. For overall gains of 7 or less the preamp clips first; above 7 the buffer clips first.

When a filter averages a signal whose peak-to-average ratio (PAR) exceeds one, A1 must not clip before A2, or the clipped part becomes an averaged output error. Both clip together when the PAR is no larger than A2's gain (2 by default); a PAR of 5 needs A2's gain raised to 5. Full-wave rectified sine has a PAR of 1.57, raised cosine 2, half-wave sine 3.14, spiky signals 10 or more.

A power switch sets the load current; the average current follows the duty cycle and gives about 100 mV average across the shunt, with peaks set by the load inductance and switching frequency. The common-mode voltage runs from about 1 V above ground (switch on) to about 1.5 V above the battery (switch off), held there by the clamp diode; a 20 V battery spike can put 21.5 V on the inputs. A gain of 40, adjustable ±5%, gives 4 V full scale with headroom to 4.4 V.

The charge kicked back by a CMOS converter's sampling capacitor can deflect the output for longer than the sample, because the open-loop output impedance is about 21 kΩ. An R-C lag network at the output, with the converter reading the capacitor, absorbs the charge; with 1 kΩ and 0.01 µF it settles in about 10 µs, so sampling every few tens of microseconds or slower causes no charge build-up.
In loops such as 4 mA to 20 mA the shunt is large enough to unbalance the input source resistances and reduce CMRR; a resistor of the shunt's value in the other input lead restores it.
